articles.title: 'An unfortunate racket': As India nears its 100th chess Grandmaster, is an expensive coach all you need?
articles.summary: Chess News: NEW DELHI: In 1978, the chess world was a reflection of a fiercely guarded aristocracy, it can be said. The title of Grandmaster (GM) was not merely a.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In 1978, the chess world was a reflection of a fiercely guarded aristocracy, it can be said. The title of Grandmaster (GM) was not merely a designation. Rather, it was an exclusive fraternity reserved for the absolute statistical anomalies of the human race.To understand what has happened to the modern chess ecosystem, one must first understand what a Grandmaster used to be. To many historians, the very definition of chess mastery has been fundamentally altered."A Grandmaster result has been a performance equivalent to a 2600 rating. In 1978, there were only six players above 2600. And in 1981, I think there were about twelve or thirteen. So a 2600 performance essentially boiled down to doing as well as the top six or seven or ten players in the world," India's veteran Grandmaster Pravin Thipsay told TimesofIndia.com during an exclusive interaction.The rating inflation over the ensuing decades has been astronomical. Thipsay believes a 2600 rating in the early 1980s was the equivalent of a 2750 rating today, a tier reserved exclusively for the absolute best in the business today.Yet, the threshold to earn the GM title remains anchored to the 2600 performance. "Which means the International Master (IM) norm in the 1980s or in the '70s was more difficult than today's Grandmaster title," Thipsay added with a smile.Many feel it has not been an organic evolution of the sport but a deliberate, commercial policy choice.Between 1914 and 1997, the world produced fewer than 300 Grandmasters. But in 1998, under the leadership of then-FIDE President Kirsan Ilyumzhinov, the governing body prioritised global expansion. The criteria for titles were relaxed, and the rating floor, once a jaw-dropping mark of 2200, was eventually plummeted to 1000 (before settling at 1400 more recently in 2024).By 2004, the world had 1,000 Grandmasters. Today, there are over 2,500."FIDE started collecting fees for rated players," Thipsay noted, outlining the financial incentive behind the dilution. "It became an important way of getting money for FIDE during Kirsan's time. He specifically made it clear in the Congress in 1998 and 2000 that we want to lower down the title, we want to lower down the rating. He said, 'We want to make everything easy for you so that you can find sponsors more easily.'"The Indian explosionAgainst this backdrop of global title inflation, India stands on the precipice of a historic milestone.In a matter of weeks, if not days, the nation will crown its 100th Grandmaster. It is a sumptuous achievement for a country that waited until 1988 for Viswanathan Anand to become its first.Today, India is an undeniable superpower as it keeps on churning out prodigies who casually dismantle the worldâs elite.But beneath the glittering surface of this golden generation lies a complex, often unspoken reality.As FIDE titles and ratings became vastly more accessible, the grassroots culture of the sport underwent a radical, heavily commercialised shift. The gritty, egalitarian days of the game have gradually evaporated, replaced by an ecosystem catered strictly to the affluent."There were tournaments where everybody played, everybody stayed in a dormitory, and 80%, 90% of the money collected would go for the prize money," Thipsay recalled. "Organisers like YMCA provided halls and dormitory accommodation free, and people didn't really bother. I remember 40, 50 people staying together for my National Juniors, and nobody really grumbled about it."Today, things are different. One-day rapid tournaments routinely charge entry fees of Rs 2,500 to Rs 5,000. Organisers rake in lakhs, while prize funds remain disproportionately small."By keeping such high entry fee, you have actually ended up making it a sport for rich people," Thipsay argued. "A common man, a child of a clerk or a laborer is not able to play even a one-day tournament irrespective of the prize. The entire chess-playing crowd has become the elite class who can afford such luxurious tournaments."The "complacency in mediocrity"Because FIDE ratings are now easily obtained, a dangerous phenomenon has taken root in Indian society. It is what Thipsay terms "complacency in mediocrity".Getting a rating today is, in his words, "probably one of the easiest things", achievable by a child after just a year of play. Yet, parents treat it as a monumental triumph.Drunk on early, low-level success, families make drastic life decisions. "Parents think, and the players think that they are good players; they are going to become Grandmasters very soon," Thipsay said."Grandmaster is everybody's ambition, whereas I think the title has not been lowered down to that level that everybody can become Grandmaster. Needless to say, there are many players who give up their studies and try their best in playing, and they end up remaining at the rating level of 1500 to 1700. Most of the players who played chess for thousands of hours, not going to school, remain between 1500 to 1800 level. And now they already have a bad academic record."With limited professional options outside the sport, these stalled players pivot to the only available avenue, which is coaching.This massive supply of trainers has birthed a sprawling, unregulated industry. Parents are liquidating assets and funnelling lakhs of rupees into private coaching, convinced it is the only path to the GM title."A need for coaching does not exist, but it is created," Thipsay, a renowned coach himself, remarked. "The way the coaching takes place is basically spoon-feeding rather than teaching chess."The doctrines of the legends like Dr Emanuel Lasker and Garry Kasparov, who preached that chess cannot merely be taught, tell us that the sole duty of a coach is to cultivate independent thinking."If you see, out of one lakh players, only three or four are able to think independently," Thipsay told this website. "We often have to de-train students for two to three years. An untrained child is much easier to teach than a trained child who is often on a wrong track."Further stressing the notion of independent thinking, he added, "Itâs very easy to become a Grandmaster if there is group discussion, if players come together, meet and discuss among themselves. All they need is the process of independent thinking. We need a coach who coaches, say, for 10 hours and teaches them to think independently."You will not have everybody becoming a Grandmaster. But many of the International Masters in the country would probably have become Grandmasters even without coaching, if they had decided to sit down together and analyse. Many of them may already be doing that as well."Itâs very easy to become a Grandmaster if there is group discussion, if players come together, meet and discuss among themselves.Nevertheless, the ongoing chess boom has perpetuated the general idea that an aspiring player must spend a heavy amount on elite coaching to reach the pinnacle."It's only a myth, and it's created to promote the coaches," Thipsay said, pointing out that players like R Praggnanandhaa, D Gukesh, and Aravindh Chithambaram became top-level Grandmasters without spending exorbitant sums on coaching early on.Furthermore, the financial return on investment is bleak.The veteran GM revealed, "The average income of an Indian Grandmaster through winnings in chess tournaments is less than one and a half lakhs per year. It's something I would call an unfortunate racket rather than expensive coaching."The pure talent argumentIs Thipsay right? Is the modern coaching industrial complex entirely a racket?Grandmaster Aravindh Chithambaram, a multiple-time National Champion known for his immense natural talent and humble beginnings, pushes back slightly on the idea that exorbitant wealth is a prerequisite, but he acknowledges the steep climb."Not necessarily I feel like one can become a Grandmaster only if he spends 20 lakhs or 30 lakhs," Aravindh told TimesofIndia.com."I think if a person is really skillful, he can achieve no matter what. But of course, the initial stages would be very hard. Because if you're not a Grandmaster or even an International Master, of course you will have to spend a lot of money. But once you make the first step, I think the rest of them would be easier comparatively. The first step would be very hard, I would say. But once you understand that you are skillful, you have the talent playing, then things are much easier."For players of Aravindh's calibre, raw skill eventually attracts sponsors, mitigating the financial burden.But for those who don't possess generation-defining talent, the necessity of a coach is less about "spoon-feeding" and more about an invaluable, finite resource like time.The pragmatic truth of the "Engine Era"Delhi's Aaryan Varshney, who recently became Indiaâs 92nd Grandmaster, offers a compelling counterweight to Thipsayâs purist philosophy.Varshneyâs journey is highly unusual. He reached the GM title at 21 without a formal academy, expensive foreign trainers, or a titled coach.Instead, he was guided entirely by his father, Gaurav, a single parent who left his job to study the game alongside his son. Yet, despite his DIY success story, Varshney is adamant that going it completely alone in the modern era is a mistake."If someone really wants to become GM, then they have to have someone who can sit with them and analyse games, sometimes all night, like my father did," Varshney told this website."A coach wouldn't necessarily do as much as my father did. But you need someone, at the very least. You can't do everything completely on your own. I didn't do anything. I'm telling you from my own experience. My father did the whole thing for me. So, doing everything yourself makes the journey difficult. You need a coach."If you're doing something yourself, something that might take us five hours, a coach can get you to do it in one hour.To Varshney, the value of a coach is not in inflating a player's ego, but in condensing the gruelling hours of modern computer engine analysis."It's not necessary for your coach to be an IM or a GM. The important thing is that the coach should be good, someone who can actually teach the child," Varshney pointed out. "If you're doing something yourself, something that might take us five hours, a coach can get you to do it in one hour. Would you rather spend five hours or one hour? Obviously, everyone would prefer one hour."Varshney's reality check underlines the modern burden placed on young players."Even analysing games yourself becomes difficult, because when you look at the engine, you can get stuck trying to understand why a particular move is good," Varshney explained. "Someone who already has that knowledge can explain it to you easily. Whatever I was struggling to understand, my father would explain it to me in two minutes. Otherwise, I would just sit there trying to figure it out."As India approaches its 100th Grandmaster, the ecosystem supporting these players remains a paradox.Thipsay is undeniably right. The title is statistically easier to obtain than it was in 1978, and the fear-mongering that demands parents spend lakhs on coaching is, in many cases, a predatory racket preying on affluent families.Yet, Varshneyâs lived experience proves that in the modern computer era, navigating the labyrinth of chess theory without a guide is a punishing task.Also Read: Gave up IIT, left home, slept on roads: How Rajasthan's first AGM put Udaipur on global chess mapA player does not need an exorbitant, six-figure coaching setup to become a Grandmaster. But they do need a translator for the digital age.India will soon celebrate its 100th Grandmaster. But behind the celebratory headlines, the true challenge will remain as to how the ecosystem ensures the sport remains a battle of minds, rather than a battle of bank accounts.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Texans Reportedly Acquire WR Kayshon Boutte From Patriots For S Jaylen Reed
articles.summary: The Houston Texans reportedly acquired wide receiver Kayshon Boutte from the New England Patriots on Monday in exchange for safety Jaylen Reed and a 2028 seventh-round draft pick.
articles.body: The Houston Texans are adding much-needed depth at wide receiver.  Houston has agreed to a deal to acquire wide receiver Kayshon Boutte from the New England Patriots in exchange for safety Jaylen Reed and a 2028 seventh-round draft pick, The Ringer reported on Monday.  The draft selection sent to New England originally belonged to the New Orleans Saints, according to NFL Network. The trade addresses an immediate roster need for Houston following a season-ending knee injury to wide receiver Jayden Higgins during last week's joint practice session with the Las Vegas Raiders. Higgins was expected to hold a starting role in the Houston offense before suffering a torn ACL. Boutte spent his first three seasons with New England after being selected in the 2023 draft. Last season, the receiver recorded 33 receptions for 551 yards and six touchdowns in a bit of a breakout year. However, Boutte became expendable this offseason following the Patriots' moves at wide receiver. They made a big trade for A.J. Brown and signed Romeo Doubs to a pricey contract. Brown and Doubs joined a wide receiver room that also features DeMario "Pop" Douglas, Kyle Williams and Mack Hollins.  So, Boutte's name emerged in trade rumors over the offseason and into training camp. He addressed the trade speculation during training camp last week. "I'm just blocking out the noise. That's the main thing. We all hear the stuff that's going on," Boutte told reporters. "But like I always said, I'm where I'm at. My feet are here, so I'm not worried about what's next or what's behind me. Just being present." In return, New England acquires Reed to bolster their secondary along with future draft compensation. Boutte now joins a Houston receiving group that features Nico Collins, Xavier Hutchinson, Jaylin Noel, and Tank Dell. articles.title: Mike McCarthy Admits Steelers, CB Joey Porter Jr. Remain At 'Impasse' Over New Deal
articles.summary: Mike McCarthy wants to work with Joey Porter Jr., but the Pittsburgh Steelers and the cornerback are at an impasse over a new deal.
articles.body: Mike McCarthy wants the chance to work with Joey Porter Jr. When McCarthy gets that chance is anyone's guess, the Pittsburgh Steelers coach included. McCarthy said Monday that the club and the fourth-year cornerback are at an impasse as the two sides try to work out a new deal. The Steelers placed Porter on the physically unable to perform list when training camp opened with what the team described as a back issue that flared up during a mobility test. It seems Porter's back problems are just part of the reason he has yet to take the practice field with the season opener against Atlanta less than three weeks away. "I learned this in my early years as a head coach, you have to separate the business from the football," McCarthy said. "Sometimes it’s easier than others." Porter is in the final season of the four-year deal he signed after the Steelers selected him with the first pick of the second round in 2023. While Pittsburgh has locked up other members of that draft class — including outside linebacker Nick Herbig and tight end Darnell Washington — Porter's status seems a little more uncertain. The 26-year-old is coming off his best season as a pro, and he said during minicamp in June that he long felt he's one of the top players at his position and that he believes he will be paid that way. The top of the cornerback market has been particularly hot of late, with Seattle’s Devon Witherspoon agreeing to a massive new deal and New England’s Christian Gonzalez getting offered one in recent weeks. Though Porter, who has three interceptions across three seasons, might not be in that neighborhood yet, he also might not be far off. Though he has deep ties to Pittsburgh — he grew up in the city while his father, Joey Porter Sr., played and then later coached for the Steelers — he didn't rush to sign his rookie deal in 2023, waiting until the eve of training camp to do it. Porter essentially "held in" during minicamp, participating in individual drills but staying out of full 11-on-11 work, a not uncommon tactic by players seeking new contracts. McCarthy described the situation as a challenge, in part because the entirety of Pittsburgh's defensive staff is in its first season. "Every one of us has a contract," McCarthy said. "The organization, they have beliefs and so forth. So that's where we are." While Porter remains out, veteran defensive back Jalen Ramsey and rookie first-round offensive tackle Max Iheanachor returned to practice on Monday. Ramsey has been on the PUP list since the start of camp because of a knee injury sustained during minicamp in June. The eight-time Pro Bowler said the defense is still getting up to speed and it's important for the entire secondary to be available when the Falcons visit on Sept. 13. "They need to pay Joey Porter," Ramsey said. Iheanachor, taken 21st overall in the draft, hadn't practiced since hurting his upper body on Aug. 6. McCarthy didn't rule out Iheanachor making an appearance when Pittsburgh wraps up the preseason on Thursday night in Buffalo. "We got two padded practices (this week), so it’ll be a really good indication of how much he’ll be able to play personally," McCarthy said. "We'll see how it goes." Reporting by the Associated Press.

articles.title: WWE Raw Live Updates, Results and Highlights From Aug. 24
articles.summary: Welcome to Bleacher Report's live coverage of WWE Raw on August 24. Scroll down for updates of all the action from Ottawa, Ontario, Canada.
articles.body:
Welcome to Bleacher Report's live coverage of WWE Raw on August 24. Scroll down for updates of all the action from Ottawa, Ontario, Canada.

OTM put Jimmy through the announce table while Keys held Jey and forced him to watch. The show ended with Knight, Solo and The Usos all down around the ring as OTM and Keys stood tall in the ring.

The Usos still had the upper hand all through the break into the next segment. They kept Sikoa isolated with quick tags and double-team moves.

The Street Champ hit a desperate clothesline to give himself some breathing room. Knight and Jimmy both tagged in at the same time. The Megastar unloaded on the elder Uso with jabs and a clothesline.

As Jey and Solo were fighting at ringside, Royce Keys put both of them through the barricade with a huge Spear. In the ring, OTM from NXT attacked Knight and Big Jim.

Bronco Nima and Lucien Price helped Keys destroy all four men. It looks like we officially have a new trio on Raw to compete with The Bloodline.

The Usos vs. LA Knight and Solo Sikoa Part 1

Jimmy and LA came out of the gate hot as soon as the bell rang. Knight hit a clothesline to get the first takedown before tagging in Solo for a double back elbow.

The Usos were able to take control with some combined attacks. They took Solo out of the ring and drilled him with a double superkick.

After a video hyping Zilla Fatu in NXT, Chad Gable was talking to Pearce backstage, and the GM said he is going to go find a new challenger for him. Ethan Page walked up and congratulated him on winning the IC title from Rey Mysterio.

All Ego said Gable is intimidated by him, but Gable reminded him that he beat him to earn the title shot in the first place. He said he would have given Page a title shot, but the way he is acting has made him change his mind.

Back in the arena, The Usos came out for their match against Sikoa and Knight.

Penta had control through the break, but the living skeleton started to regain his footing. He took Penta down with a few high-flying moves and scored a two-count with a powerslam.

La Parka drilled the former IC champion with a DDT for a close two-count. Penta caught him with a Penta Driver, but he couldn't keep him down for the pin.

A Spanish Fly got La Parka another near-fall before Penta wrenched his arm behind his back. He hit the Mexican Destroyer to seal the victory and advance to the finals.

This was a solid match, but the most intriguing part of this is that we will see Penta and Fenix fight in the finals next week to determine who gets to face Roman Reigns for the world title in Mexico City.

Lyra Valkyria had a brief exchange with Sol Ruca and Iyo Sky before Penta made his way out first to take on La Parka in the other semifinal match in the ongoing No. 1 Contender's tournament.

The luchadores started with a fast-paced exchange, but Penta took control. He sent La Parka out of the ring so he could take him down with a dive through the ropes.

La Parka recovered and hit a moonsault from the middle rope to the floor. Penta caught him with a superkick as he was coming off the top rope, but it only got him a two-count.

We returned to see Cass missing a corner splash. Evans tried to build a little momentum, but he couldn't take Cass off his feet. The big man caught him, but Evans sent him over the top rope before hitting a suicide dive.

The Young OG put Cass in the timekeeper's area so he could hit a running dive over the barricade. Evans started unloading on him with punches and kicks.

He brought Cass back in the ring and hit the Red Dot kick and a springboard clothesline. He went for the OG Cutter, but Cass shoved him off the top turnbuckle.

He nailed Je'Von with a big boot for the win. This seemed like a pretty abrupt ending, and an odd choice for a finishing move.

Judgment Day attacked Evans after Cass left the ring and left him down and out.

Big Cass has been making Evans' life hard recently, so they met in what was the first match Cass has had in WWE since returning. The way they shot the entrance for Cass was designed to make him look as big as possible, and it worked.

Evans tried to stick and move to avoid the big man. He brought the powerhouse out of the ring with a hurricanrana, but when he went for a slingshot crossbody, Cass caught him. Je'Von got back in the ring and Cass leveled him with a clothesline over the top rope.

Michael Cole talked about the journey Cass has been on since he was fired by WWE eight years ago as we saw him throw Evans into the barricade. He said Cass has taken no accountability for his actions.

Paul Heyman and Adam Pearce were in the ring for a contract signing between Oba Femi and Bron Breakker. The Ruler made his entrance first as the crowd chanted his name.

Breakker asked Femi who he thinks he is, claiming to be the future. He asked what Femi has done to earn the title of being the future of WWE. He diminished Femi's King of the Ring win and victory over Brock Lesnar.

He talked a lot of trash about how Femi wouldn't even be where he is if Breakker hadn't been out with an injury for months. The Ruler called him an angry, orange man and said he can't understand that his chances of being the face of WWE are gone.

Breakker signed the contract and said Femi is going to realize he is the one guy he can't beat. He taunted Oba by saying Heyman should sign it for him since they are so close now.

Bron and Oba ended up brawling after Breakker threatened Heyman. Austin Theory showed up to help his partner, but Femi fought them off and put Theory through the table.

We returned to see both men trading chops. Lee hit a few kicks to take Fenix off his feet. He hit a beautiful float over into a powerbomb, but it couldn't get him the win.

They continued to trade fast-paced offense until they ended up fighting near the announce table. Fenix was tripped on the table, which gave Lee an opening to hit a massive cannonball through the second rope that hit Fenix off the top of the table.

That spot was wild! The crowd chanted "This is awesome" as Lee brought Fenix in for a tornado DDT to get a two-count. Rey hit a brainbuster as he began regaining momentum.

He got Lee up for the Mexican Muscle Buster, but Lee countered into the Styles Clash for a near-fall. They kept going back and forth until Fenix finally hit his finisher to get the win.

This match was incredible. If you are not watching the show live, make sure you check this one out. Both guys worked their butts off to make this awesome.

The No. 1 Contender's tournament continued this week with Rey Fenix taking on Dragon Lee in the semifinals. Before the match, Je'Von Evans attacked Dom Mysterio and JD McDonagh backstage, which Rey Mysterio seemed to love.

They started with a quick exchange of holds and counters. Neither man could get an advantage as they went move for move. They came to a stalemate before they began trading strikes.

Lee was the first one to take control with a nice dropkick in the corner for a two-count, but Fenix wasn't down for long. He hit the running kick across the top rope he is known for, and he followed it with a diving crossbody for a near-fall.

The AAA cruiserweight champion hit a moonsault on the floor, but when they got back into the ring, Lee hit a German suplex. He took Fenix down with a huge dive over the top rope that sent us into the break.

Perez had control through the break, but Vaquer was starting to make a comeback when we returned. Roxy had to pull her hair to escape an abdominal stretch, but the former world champion maintained control.

She used the Devil's Kiss to slam Roxanne's head into the mat 10 times. She used a brutal dragon screw leg whip in the corner before hitting a running double knee against the turnbuckle.

Perez recovered and hit a nice shining wizard for a two-count. Stephanie countered a crossface into a package backbreaker. Morgan interfered while Rodriguez distracted the ref. This brought out Becky Lynch.

Roxy tried to take advantage of all the mayhem, but Vaquer was able to hit her with her finisher to score the win.

Lynch took Morgan out at ringside before getting into the ring. She and Vaquer exchanged a few words before The Man made her exit.

Stephanie Vaquer vs. Roxanne Perez Part 1

Stephanie Vaquer returned to action for the first time since WrestleMania to take on Roxanne Perez. La Primera made her way to the ring right before the break. Liv Morgan and Raquel Rodriguez were at ringside.

Perez played some mind games by avoiding Vaquer a few times before slapping her and then hiding in the ropes. Once Vaquer got her hands on her, she wrestled her to the mat and stomped on her elbow.
